standard.title: Efficient addition and multiplication strategies
standard.description: Develop efficient strategies and use appropriate digital tools for solving problems involving addition and subtraction, and multiplication and division where there is no remainder
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value (AC9M3N03) and multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers (AC9M3N04). They have not yet developed efficient strategies for multi-digit multiplication or applied digital tools strategically.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop and apply efficient strategies for addition, subtraction, multiplication and division problems with larger numbers, selecting strategies appropriately and using digital tools where helpful.

nodes.label: Efficient addition and subtraction strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply and explain at least two efficient strategies for multi-digit addition or subtraction.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply one strategy beyond the standard algorithm (e.g. compensation, near-hundreds) to solve one addition or subtraction problem; explain why this approach is efficient.
nodes.typical_width: Develop, apply and explain multiple efficient strategies for addition and subtraction (partitioning, compensation, near-numbers, constant difference for subtraction); select strategies based on the numbers involved; use digital tools to verify.
wider: Compare the efficiency of different strategies for the same problem type (e.g. 497 + 348: partition vs compensation) and build a decision rule for when each strategy is more efficient
Apply strategies to multi-step problems where an efficient approach for each sub-step reduces overall cognitive load

response_modes.reason: Efficient computation requires a repertoire of strategies, not a single approach. Students who know only one method (e.g. always partition) are less flexible than those who can select from compensation, near-hundreds or constant difference depending on the numbers.

success_criteria: Students can apply at least two different efficient strategies for multi-digit addition or subtraction
Students can explain why a chosen strategy is efficient for a given pair of numbers

nodes.label: Multiplication strategies for larger numbers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply area model or partitioning strategies to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number.
nodes.minimum_width: Use place value partitioning to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number (e.g. 34 × 6 = 30×6 + 4×6); record and explain the steps.
nodes.typical_width: Develop and apply efficient strategies for multiplication including area models, partitioning and the distributive property; extend to two-digit by two-digit multiplication using arrays or area models; use digital tools to check solutions.
wider: Use an area model to connect multiplication of two-digit numbers to the distributive property — showing how the grid squares represent the partial products
Investigate which strategies are most efficient for different types of multiplication problems (e.g. near-doubles, using known facts as anchors for derived facts)

response_modes.reason: Area models and partitioning require students to keep track of partial products — the reasoning scaffold (recording each step, labelling which part of the grid corresponds to which calculation) is necessary to prevent errors that accumulate from informal mental approaches.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multiplication strategies with the area model and distributive property provide a rich conceptual foundation for multi-digit multiplication algorithms in later years and for algebra. Students who engage deeply here have a visual model they can apply to abstract expressions.
success_criteria: Students can multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number using a partitioning strategy, recording each step
Students can explain the connection between their calculation and the area model or array

nodes.label: Division without remainders
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can solve division problems without remainders using known multiplication facts and sharing/grouping strategies.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve one division problem without a remainder using known multiplication facts or equal sharing (e.g. 48 ÷ 6 by thinking 'what times 6 equals 48?').
nodes.typical_width: Solve division problems without remainders using inverse multiplication, grouping and sharing; represent with arrays; use digital tools to check; select efficient strategies based on the size of numbers and available facts.
wider: Investigate the two meanings of division (equal sharing vs equal grouping) using the same problem, and discuss when each interpretation is more natural in context
Connect division to fraction notation — 12 ÷ 4 = 1/4 of 12 = 3 — building the fraction-as-division understanding
success_criteria: Students can solve a division problem without a remainder using an appropriate strategy
Students can explain whether they are finding the number of groups or the size of each group
